questions.question: What does a Rails controller do?
questions.title: Rails Controllers
questions.direct_answer: A controller is the traffic cop of MVC: it receives a request (with params), asks the model for data, and renders a response. A controller is a class inheriting from ApplicationController, with one method per action (index, show, create); each action sets up instance variables (@post = Post.find(params[:id])) and renders (explicitly or by convention — render :show by default). Controllers hold NO business logic — that lives in models or service objects; the controller orchestrates (find, authorize, call a service, render). Strong params (params.require(:post).permit(:title)) guard mass-assignment. Keep controllers thin: find, authorize, delegate, render.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know a controller receives params, talks to models, and renders; that actions are methods; and that controllers should be thin (no business logic).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting business logic in controllers (they should delegate to models/services), or forgetting strong params (mass-assignment risk).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: A controller receives params, asks models for data, and renders. Actions are methods. Controllers are thin: find, authorize, delegate, render. Strong params guard mass-assignment.

sections.title: The Traffic Cop of MVC
sections.content: A controller is the traffic cop of MVC: it receives a request (with params), asks the model for data, and renders a response. A controller is a class inheriting from ApplicationController, with one method per action (index, show, create); each action sets up instance variables (@post = Post.find(params id)) and renders, explicitly or by convention — render show by default. Controllers hold NO business logic — that lives in models or service objects; the controller orchestrates: find, authorize, call a service, render. Strong params (params dot require post dot permit title) guard mass-assignment. Keep controllers thin: find, authorize, delegate, render.

sections.title: Request -> Controller -> Response
sections.content:
A controller receives params, finds models, and renders.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R[request + params] --> A[action: index/show/create]
  A --> M[find/authorize: @post = Post.find]
  M --> De[delegate to model/service]
  De --> Re[render json / render :show]
```

sections.title: A Rails controller
sections.content:
```ruby
class PostsController < ApplicationController
  # GET /posts (params: ?page=)
  def index
    @posts = Post.page(params[:page])   # find (model)
    # render :index by convention (HTML) OR:
    render json: @posts                  # API
  end

  # GET /posts/:id
  def show
    @post = Post.find(params[:id])       # find
    # render :show by convention
  end

  # POST /posts (params: { post: { title, body } })
  def create
    @post = Post.create!(post_params)    # delegate to model
    redirect_to @post                    # render: redirect
  end

  private
  # Strong params: guard mass-assignment
  def post_params
    params.require(:post).permit(:title, :body)
  end
end
# Controllers are THIN: find, authorize, delegate, render. No business logic.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Putting business logic in controllers — delegate to models/services.
Forgetting strong params — mass-assignment security risk.
Setting too many instance variables (@x) — a sign the view needs a presenter.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A controller receives a request (params), asks models for data, and renders a response.
Actions are methods (index, show, create); @vars are passed to the view.
Controllers are thin: find, authorize, delegate to a model/service, render.
render is explicit (render json:) or by convention (render :show by default).

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A controller is the traffic cop of MVC: it receives a request (with params), asks the model for data, and renders a response. A controller is a class inheriting from ApplicationController, with one method per action (index, show, create); each action sets up instance variables (@post = Post.find params id) and renders, explicitly or by convention — render show by default. Controllers hold NO business logic — that lives in models or service objects; the controller orchestrates: find, authorize, call a service, render. Strong params (params dot require post dot permit title) guard mass-assignment. Keep controllers thin: find, authorize, delegate, render. A common mistake is putting business logic in controllers, when they should delegate to models and services, and forgetting strong params, which is a mass-assignment risk.
